analysis.one_liner: Lets states extend public children's health coverage to families at four times the poverty level and subsidize private job-based plans.
analysis.headline: The bill died without any vote: referred to the House Energy and Commerce Committee in March 2007 and sent to its Health Subcommittee, where it sat until the Congress ended in January 2009.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would have let states use the Children's Health Insurance Program (SCHIP) to cover children in families earning up to 400% of the federal poverty line, with open-ended federal funding for states that expanded and imposed no enrollment caps. It would have subsidized children's job-based coverage, required dental and health-center services in SCHIP plans, let states cover older young adults, legal-immigrant children, and low-income pregnant women, and simplified enrollment by letting families qualify through other benefit programs like school lunch. It never received a hearing, a committee vote, or a floor vote.
analysis.who_benefits: Uninsured and underinsured children in families earning up to four times the poverty line, whose states could enroll them in SCHIP; low-income pregnant women and legal-immigrant children, whom states could newly cover; young adults up to age 25, whom states could extend Medicaid to; and families who would get federal help paying premiums for job-based coverage for their kids.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Children in low- and middle-income families

how_it_helps.text: Lets any state raise SCHIP eligibility for children from 200% to up to 400% of the poverty line, and the state's federal allotment increases by whatever sums are necessary to pay for the expansion, so money cannot run out mid-year.
States that expand coverage, keep enrollment open with no caps or waiting lists, and simplify applications get an increased federal matching rate for children's Medicaid care.

Requires SCHIP benchmark plans to cover early and periodic screening, diagnostic, and treatment services including dental care, plus federally-qualified health center and rural health clinic services, at full actuarial value.

Lets states cover young adults up to age 25 under Medicaid and SCHIP, cover lawfully residing immigrant children and pregnant women, and cover targeted low-income pregnant women, with newborns automatically enrolled at birth.

Creates an 'express lane' so a child already found eligible for food stamps, school lunch, or other public assistance can be enrolled in Medicaid or SCHIP without a duplicate application, and pays 90% federal match for school-based outreach.
Rebases SCHIP funding on health care cost and child population growth, allows two-year use of allotments, and redirects unused state allotments to states facing funding shortfalls.

analysis.who_pays: Federal taxpayers, through an uncapped appropriation for states that expand eligibility to 400% of poverty plus higher matching rates and enlarged allotments; the bill specifies no dedicated revenue source.

drawbacks.text: The federal funding for states expanding to 400% of poverty is open-ended ('such sums as may be necessary'), with no dedicated financing in the bill, so the cost to taxpayers was unquantified at introduction.

Subsidies for employment-based coverage route federal money through private employer plans and would cover some middle-income children who already had or could obtain private coverage, raising the risk of the government substituting for premiums families or employers would otherwise pay.

Federal matching payments for employer-coverage subsidies are capped at 50% of what SCHIP would otherwise spend on the child, and the purchase-of-coverage option for families above the eligibility line gets no federal match at all, so higher-income families would pay community-rated premiums.
The bill gives states the option to require documentary proof of citizenship for Medicaid, a requirement critics linked to eligible citizens losing coverage when they cannot produce documents.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The coverage gains are substantial and well-targeted at uninsured children, and the simplified enrollment and dependable funding provisions address real gaps that caused children to lose coverage. The main weakness is financing: an uncapped federal appropriation with no revenue source means the true cost would have been settled elsewhere, and the employer-coverage subsidies partially substitute public money for premiums that families and employers would otherwise pay. On balance the benefits to children's coverage are large, but the bill as introduced left its cost unaddressed.

outcome.mechanism: It was sent to the House Energy and Commerce Committee and then to its Health Subcommittee in March 2007, and no one ever brought it to a hearing, a committee vote, or the floor before the two-year Congress ended.

narrative.text: The bill was introduced on March 15, 2007 by Rep. John Dingell with 22 original cosponsors and referred to the House Committee on Energy and Commerce.

The next day it was referred to the Subcommittee on Health, where it stayed; the action history shows no hearing, no markup, no committee vote, and no floor action for the remainder of the 110th Congress.
The bill's committee assignment list contains only the referral to Energy and Commerce, and no committee or floor votes are recorded for it.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: No constituency ever had to vote on the comprehensive expansion, so opponents of extending public coverage up the income scale and of uncapped federal health spending were spared a recorded position, while families of uninsured children gained nothing because the bill never became law. (Separately that Congress, SCHIP reauthorization moved through other bills.)

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Opponents of coverage expansion avoided a vote

for.name: Rep. John D. Dingell
for.role: U.S. Representative (D-MI), Chair of the House Energy and Commerce Committee
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and referred it to his own committee; it never emerged from its Health Subcommittee.

for.name: 43 of 233 House Democrats
for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill; all 43 cosponsors were Democrats.

against.name: House Energy and Commerce Subcommittee on Health
against.what_they_did: Received the referral on March 16, 2007 and never held a hearing or acted on the bill for the rest of the Congress.

against.name: House Committee on Energy and Commerce
against.what_they_did: Never reported the bill out; it never reached a committee vote or the House floor.

sides.party_line_note: No votes were ever taken, so no roll-call split exists; sponsorship was entirely Democratic, with all 43 cosponsors Democrats and no Republican cosponsors listed.

industries.note: The bill lets states use SCHIP dollars to subsidize children's enrollment in job-based group health plans, with federal matching at up to half the cost, creating paying customers for employer plans and the insurers that cover them while helping families afford premiums.

industries.industry: Federally-qualified health centers and rural health clinics
industries.note: SCHIP benchmark plans would be required to cover health center and rural clinic services, guaranteeing reimbursement for care delivered to enrolled children.
The bill requires SCHIP coverage of EPSDT services including dental care, extending paid dental treatment to newly covered children.

States choosing to expand would receive open-ended federal payments, higher matching rates, rebased allotments growing with health costs and enrollment, and redistribution of unused funds from other states.
